entries.name: Sequre
entries.summary: A statically compiled Pythonic framework for secure computation pipelines, combining secure multiparty computation, homomorphic encryption and multiparty homomorphic encryption in one system, with built-in linear algebra, statistics and machine learning. Codon is both the compilation target and an extension point: 130 .codon files compile to native code through Codon with no interpreter, and the repo additionally carries C++ sources against Codon's IR (ir/helpers/bet.h, ir/helpers/utils.cpp), so Sequre ships a compiler pass as well as a library.
entries.why_codon: README states programs compile to native machine code via Codon with no runtime interpreter overhead, and that the result outperforms interpreter-based MPC frameworks by orders of magnitude.

entries.name: Shechi
entries.summary: An end-to-end statically compiled Pythonic framework for multiparty homomorphic encryption pipelines, distributed as an anonymous conference artifact with a prepared container image. The codebase is a snapshot of Sequre: 87 of its 88 .codon files share paths with 0xTCG/sequre and 20 are byte-identical, its container mounts a /sequre working directory, and it carries the same Codon IR C++ helpers. Codon is the compilation target throughout.
entries.why_codon: README claims a statically compiled, performance-engineered framework; no Codon-specific benchmark claim is made in the repo itself.

paper.note: no paper DOI; six Zenodo artifact DOIs exist

entries.ruling: Kept as its own entry rather than folded into Sequre: two distinct papers on a shared codebase, so the SDV published-survives rule does not apply. The shared code is recorded by derived_from.

entries.name: Vectron
entries.summary: A compiler pass that analyses array- and matrix-based dynamic programming kernels and vectorizes them automatically, reporting up to 18x throughput improvement on DP algorithms. Vectron is written as a Codon extension: its 151 .codon files carry the dispatcher, the attribute machinery and a large set of generated CPU and GPU alignment kernels, and it depends on a from-source Codon build with its LLVM distribution.
entries.why_codon: Vectron is built as a Codon compiler pass; the repo states the vectorizer improves DP performance up to 18 times.

paper.title: Vectron: A Dynamic Programming Auto-vectorization Framework

entries.name: Conduit
entries.summary: A web framework for machine-learning APIs, MCP servers and streaming services, describing itself as AI-first and claiming native performance. Codon is the implementation language: 151 .codon files hold the HTTP server, middleware, MCP protocol handling and tooling, with sockets bound through from-C-import and a NumPy path used for the inference demos.
entries.why_codon: Repo claims native performance for a Python-shaped web framework; badge pins Codon 0.16+.
entries.note: README carries an MIT license badge linking to LICENSE, but the repo contains no LICENSE file.

entries.name: FLOX
entries.summary: A framework for building trading systems -- strategies, backtests, paper trading and live execution behind one toolkit, distributed on PyPI and npm. Codon is the scripting surface over a C or C++ core rather than the whole system: 55 .codon files hold the strategy, backtest, order-book and execution modules, and 28 of them declare 1,347 C entry points through Codon's from-C-import interop.
entries.why_codon: No Codon performance claim appears anywhere in the repo. Inferred from the binding layer: 1,347 from-C-import declarations across 28 files place Codon as the native-speed strategy surface over the C core.

entries.name: scATAC-seq (StarScope)
entries.summary: A single-cell ATAC-seq processing pipeline documented at the StarScope site. It both vendors and uses Codon: 71 stdlib files plus the Codon parser headers and the jit Python package are committed into the repo, and on top of that sit 24 of its own .codon files holding the barcode and alignment work. The Seq plugin carries the sequence handling, with 56 from-C-import declarations concentrated in three files.
entries.why_codon: README is a pointer to the documentation site and makes no Codon claim. Inferred from the vendored toolchain and the Seq plugin usage that Codon runs the sequence-processing stages of the pipeline.
entries.note: Vendors more than an install: codon/include/codon/parser/ headers and codon/python/codon/decorator.py are present, so the Codon source tree and the jit package are both committed.

entries.name: fastcodon
entries.summary: FastAPI rebuilt natively in Codon so that an ASGI-class web framework compiles to machine code, developed bottom-up against a published dependency graph with each layer marked verified as it lands. Sixty-four .codon files carry the stack from non-blocking sockets and a poll-based selector up through pure-Codon SHA-1, SHA-256, HMAC and base64, an HTTP parser, cancel scopes and task groups, chunked streaming and a WebSocket transport. The 57 from-C-import declarations sit in five files and are the platform boundary, covering both Winsock and BSD sockets.
entries.why_codon: README states the framework is rebuilt natively in Codon so that it compiles to machine code and runs at native speed.
entries.note: Writes its own crypto and socket layers in Codon rather than binding a C library, so it exercises the language more broadly than its single recorded feature suggests.

entries.name: CSC427 Fall 2025 (Exophobias)
entries.summary: Coursework for UVic's Fall 2025 CSC427 bioinformatics course, organised week by week with a final project. The largest of the student repos: 37 .codon files covering genome assembly, motif matrices, alignment and a Codon port of scanpy preprocessing, with 85 Python interop sites across seventeen files as ported library code reaches back into Python.
entries.why_codon: Course assignments require porting Python bioinformatics code to Codon and comparing runtimes. Inferred from the weekly structure and the CI harness, which installs Codon and Seq and runs both versions.

entries.name: CSC427 Fall 2025 (kellofoggs)
entries.summary: Coursework for UVic's Fall 2025 CSC427 bioinformatics course. Twenty-four .codon files across the weekly assignments, with 25 Python interop sites and the widest NumPy usage of the student repos at ten sites across eight files.
entries.why_codon: Course requirement. Inferred from the same weekly structure and CI harness as the other student repos.

entries.name: CSC427 Fall 2025 (liamsquires)
entries.summary: Coursework for UVic's Fall 2025 CSC427 bioinformatics course. Fifteen .codon files, including a genome-assembly week with a de Bruijn graph keyed on k-mers and a phylogenetic tree implementation.
entries.why_codon: Course requirement. Inferred from the weekly structure and the shared CI harness.

entries.name: CSC427 Fall 2025 (Milorph)
entries.summary: Coursework for UVic's Fall 2025 CSC427 bioinformatics course. Nineteen .codon files spanning the trviz, biopython and alignment weeks.
entries.why_codon: Course requirement. Inferred from the weekly structure and the shared CI harness.

entries.name: Single Cell Toolkit
entries.summary: A set of command-line tools for single-cell ATAC FASTQ handling, chiefly attaching 10x cell barcodes from one read file onto the paired reads and correcting them against a whitelist. Nine .codon files carry the barcode extraction and correction, and it is the heaviest user of the Seq plugin found so far, with 41 bio-import sites across all nine files and the pipeline operator used for k-mer mutation.
entries.why_codon: README documents shell usage only and makes no Codon claim. Inferred from the Seq plugin and pipeline usage that Codon runs the per-read barcode work.

entries.name: Decor
entries.summary: A framework for evaluating non-linear functions inside secure multiparty computation, covering Chebyshev approximation, logistic regression, neural network layers and GWAS, MNIST and SIREN applications. Codon is reached through Sequre rather than directly: installation pins Codon v0.17.0, drops the Sequre release into the Codon plugin directory, and runs every program as codon run -plugin sequre.
entries.why_codon: README makes no performance claim for Codon; it pins Codon v0.17.0 as the runtime and loads Sequre as a Codon plugin. Inferred from the install recipe that Codon is the execution substrate.

entries.name: codon-numpy
entries.summary: A NumPy implementation delivered as a Codon compiler plugin. It carries no README; the structure is the documentation. A C++ class deriving from codon::DSL registers IR passes through codon/dsl/dsl.h, a plugin.toml declares the plugin, and six .codon files under stdlib/numpy supply ndarray, array creation, reductions, BLAS and linalg. The first pure compiler-plugin entry in the index -- Sequre ships IR helpers alongside a library, whereas this repo is only the plugin.
entries.why_codon: No README and no claim anywhere. Inferred from the codon::DSL subclass and plugin.toml that the repo exists to extend Codon itself rather than to use it.
entries.note: Possible lineage worth checking with him: the author is a co-author on the Codon and Sequre papers, this repo stopped in 2023, and Codon's own stdlib now carries a numpy package whose module names overlap (ndarray, create, reductions, linalg). Recorded as an observation, not a causal claim.

entries.name: CSC427 Fall 2025 (reedbryan)
entries.summary: Coursework for UVic's Fall 2025 CSC427 bioinformatics course. Seventeen .codon files using no Codon-specific feature at all -- straight Python ported across and compiled, which is the assignment's point.
entries.why_codon: Course requirement. Inferred from the weekly structure and the shared CI harness.

entries.name: CSC427 Fall 2025 (tristancornwell)
entries.summary: Coursework for UVic's Fall 2025 CSC427 bioinformatics course. Fourteen .codon files, with the alignment week carrying both global and affine-gap implementations.
entries.why_codon: Course requirement. Inferred from the weekly structure and the shared CI harness.

entries.name: TrESFlow
entries.summary: A Nextflow DSL2 pipeline built on the nf-core template for preprocessing TrES-seq data. Codon supplies the per-read core: six .codon files under scripts/core_runtime handle read splitting, FASTQ to SAM conversion and the tagging steps for UMIs and ligation sites, using the Seq plugin throughout and the pipeline operator in the splitting stage.
entries.why_codon: README documents the Nextflow pipeline and does not mention Codon. Inferred from the scripts/core_runtime tree and its Seq plugin usage that Codon runs the per-read stages inside the workflow.

entries.name: BISER
entries.summary: A tool for detecting and decomposing segmental duplications in one genome or across many, successor to SEDEF, distributed on PyPI. All six of its bio-import sites sit in its eight .codon files, and building from source requires Codon together with the Seq plugin.
entries.why_codon: README makes no Codon performance claim; it names Codon plus the Seq plugin as the from-source build requirement. Inferred from the Seq plugin dependency that Codon is used for the sequence-processing core.

entries.name: MCE Sandbox
entries.summary: A sandbox comparing prime-sieve implementations across Perl with MCE and Inline::C, C with OpenMP, and Codon. Seven .codon files carry the sieve variants, and they are the reason Codon is present: primes2 reimplements the reference algorithm, primes4 drives the libprimesieve C API, and the cpusieve, gpusieve and pgpusieve trio walk the same range sieve from CPU parallelism up to Codon's @par(gpu=True) form. Second GPU-annotated Codon code found in the index.
entries.why_codon: README names Codon as one of the three implementation technologies under comparison and labels each Codon variant by what it exercises, including the @par(gpu=True) syntax.

entries.name: Minimap2 in Codon (CSC 427)
entries.summary: A reimplementation of Minimap2's core features in Python compiled with Codon, written for a CSC 427 student project and aiming to be more readable than the original C. Thirteen .codon files hold the sketching, indexing and utility layers, with 24 Seq plugin imports spread across twelve of them -- the widest per-file Seq usage in the index.
entries.why_codon: README states the project implements Minimap2 in Python compiled with Codon, for readability over the C original.

entries.name: CSC427 Fall 2025 (rachel-wenhui-ma)
entries.summary: Coursework for UVic's Fall 2025 CSC427 bioinformatics course. Nine .codon files, the smallest of the student repos that still carries Codon sources.
entries.why_codon: Course requirement. Inferred from the weekly structure and the shared CI harness.

entries.name: Secure MICE
entries.summary: An implementation of secure multiple imputation with chained equations, benchmarked against non-secure baselines from a companion notebook. The repo states it is implemented as an integral part of the Sequre framework, so Codon is reached through Sequre: four .codon files hold the application, and the benchmark container carries Codon debug settings rather than invoking Codon directly.
entries.why_codon: README makes no Codon claim at all; it positions the work inside Sequre. Inferred from the Sequre dependency and the CODON_DEBUG setting in the benchmark command that Codon is the compilation substrate.

entries.name: TurboX (sir-george2500)
entries.summary: A Python backend framework built on the Codon compiler, layered over a server core called Nucleus that is itself written in Codon with C FFI. Nine .codon files hold the application layer and the server core; the six from-C-import sites are spread one per file rather than concentrated in a binding module.
entries.why_codon: README states TurboX leverages Codon to compile Python code to machine code, delivering performance comparable to Rust and C++ without traditional interpreter overhead.
entries.note: Shares a name with cruso003/TurboX and nothing else: the two have zero .codon paths in common and different layouts. Not a fork.

entries.name: RDI (Repeat Detection Index)
entries.summary: A library that builds an index for finding repeated substrings and uses it for de novo genome assembly, describing itself as a Codon library. Fourteen .codon files hold the suffix array, LCP, k-mer, B-tree and Bloom filter machinery; the Seq plugin supplies the sequence types and Python interop is used to reach json, bz2, tqdm and argparse from inside Codon.
entries.why_codon: README states RDI is a Codon library and requires Codon with Python interoperability enabled plus the Seq plugin.

entries.name: GraphMemory-IDE
entries.summary: A long-term memory system for IDEs built over the Kuzu graph database. Codon carries the compute-heavy layer rather than the application: four graph kernels covering centrality, community detection, similarity and path analysis, plus hashing and vector operations under data_processing, with a dedicated Dockerfile for the Codon build.
entries.why_codon: README describes the system without naming Codon. Inferred from the codon/graph_kernels and codon/data_processing trees and the dedicated Dockerfile.codon that Codon is the acceleration layer for graph analytics.

entries.name: Triton-Seq
entries.summary: A GPU framework for Smith-Waterman sequence alignment built on Triton kernels with custom MLIR compiler passes for shared-memory optimization. Codon is not the implementation: it is one of six alternatives the project evaluates alongside Triton, TileLang, ThunderKittens, CuTile and native CUDA, and its nine .codon files sit under experiments/codon and experiments/dsl_comparison. They are nonetheless the only GPU-annotated Codon code found in the index so far.
entries.why_codon: README lists Codon among the DSLs evaluated and implemented against for comparison; no claim is made that Codon powers the framework.

entries.name: codon-light
entries.summary: A retargeted build of Codon's C++ runtime, carrying Exaloop's own lib.h and exception machinery with CMake configurations for desktop, WebAssembly and bare metal. The single .codon file is a replacement threading module supplying ThreadLocal and the lock primitives against the reduced runtime. It does not use Codon to build something; it changes where Codon-compiled code can run.
entries.why_codon: No README. Inferred from the baremetal, wasm and desktop CMake targets over Codon's runtime sources that the aim is to run Codon output in constrained environments.

entries.name: scPreproc
entries.summary: A single-cell preprocessing pipeline whose demultiplexing stage is written in Codon. Two .codon files hold the work, run through the Seq plugin with compile-time parameters supplied on the command line -- barcode length, barcode start offset and a minimum read threshold are passed as -D definitions, so the barcode geometry is fixed at compile time rather than read at runtime.
entries.why_codon: README instructs the user to install Codon and Seq and gives the exact codon run -plugin seq -release command line; it makes no performance claim.

entries.name: scalce_codon
entries.summary: A reimplementation of the SCALCE FASTQ compression algorithm in Codon, run through the Seq plugin. Four .codon files carry the Aho-Corasick trie, the pattern set and the compression and decompression paths.
entries.why_codon: README states it is a reimplementation of SCALCE in Codon and gives the codon run -plugin seq invocation.

entries.name: TurboX (cruso003)
entries.summary: An alpha web framework built on the Codon compiler with first-class MCP support, pinning Codon 0.16 or later. Sixteen .codon files hold examples and feature tests rather than a large framework body, and the ten from-C-import sites are confined to two files. By the same author as Conduit, which is larger, later and carries the same MCP framing.
entries.why_codon: README states it compiles Python-like code to native machine code via Codon, claiming performance comparable to Go and Rust and 10-100x faster than CPython.
entries.note: README carries an MIT license badge linking to LICENSE, but the repo contains no LICENSE file. Conduit, by the same author, has the same discrepancy.

entries.name: tsp-solver
entries.summary: Metaheuristics for the travelling salesman problem, the main line of work written in Python across several local-search variants. A single .codon file ports the naive local-search solver; no other variant has a Codon counterpart.
entries.why_codon: README documents the Python variants only and never mentions Codon. Inferred from the single .codon port of tsp_ls_naive that Codon was tried on one solver; no timing or comparison is published in the repo.
entries.note: Filed exploration rather than benchmark: a Python counterpart exists, but the repo publishes no comparison.

entries.name: md5-codon
entries.summary: An MD5 implementation in Codon that publishes its own measurements: 1.5x to 2.0x faster than hashlib.md5 and 1.1x to 1.2x faster than a Codon-plus-Python implementation. Three .codon files hold the digest, a test harness and a Codon-Python comparison, with ten inline LLVM sites across two of them.
entries.why_codon: README reports the speedups directly against hashlib.md5 and against a Codon-plus-Python implementation.

entries.name: Benchmarking Mojo
entries.summary: A cross-language benchmark suite written for a 2024 Bachelor's thesis on Mojo, run from a Docker image over softmax, quicksort, matmul and crc16. Codon is one of the languages measured rather than the subject: five .codon files hold the four algorithms plus a shared bench_suite harness.
entries.why_codon: README frames the repo as benchmarking Mojo; Codon appears as one of the compared languages. No Codon-specific claim is made.
entries.note: Bachelor's thesis work rather than a taught-course exercise; filed as coursework because no separate thesis value exists in the vocabulary.

entries.name: phaseProject
entries.summary: A rudimentary simulation of a phase transition with pygame visualization. One .codon file holds the simulation, reaching pygame and the rest of the visualization stack through eight Python interop imports -- the densest use of Python interop per file in the index.
entries.why_codon: README describes the simulation without naming Codon. Inferred from the single Codon source driving a pygame loop through Python interop that Codon supplies the simulation speed while Python supplies the graphics.

entries.name: takechi-scratch/atcoder
entries.summary: Competitive programming solutions for AtCoder contests. Codon enters through the site's May 2025 language test, where four .codon files solve the standard practice problems, with one further solution filed under a recent contest round.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from the language-test-202505 directory that Codon is being trialled as an AtCoder submission language.

entries.name: DS Tools
entries.summary: Small helper binaries for pre- and post-processing datasets, split into combine_csv and split_csv with their own argument handling. The README says plainly that the tools are written in Codon just out of fun, and calls the language experimental.
entries.why_codon: README states the tools are written in the experimental language Codon just out of fun; no performance claim is made.

entries.name: strings.codon
entries.summary: A Codon reimplementation of the Unix strings utility, one file, with seven C entry points bound for the file and memory handling.
entries.why_codon: README is the title only. Inferred from the repo being a single-purpose Codon port of a Unix utility that the aim is a native-speed reimplementation.

entries.name: markhend/aoc
entries.summary: Advent of Code solutions kept across many languages, one directory per year and day. Codon is one of the languages exercised: seven .codon files spread over the 2020 and 2021 puzzles, each a standalone solution using no Codon-specific feature.
entries.why_codon: No claim and no comparison prose. Inferred from the polyglot layout that Codon is being tried as one solution language among many.

entries.name: yogi
entries.summary: A small typed input-reading package for beginners, distributed on PyPI by the Jutge.org online judge so that students get static type checking on the data they read. Alongside the Python implementation sits a single .codon port of the same interface, so a student solution written in Codon can use the identical reading API.
entries.why_codon: README documents the Python package only. Inferred from the parallel yogi.codon port that Jutge supports Codon submissions and needs the same input interface there.

entries.name: Awesome Mojo
entries.summary: A curated list of Mojo code and problem solutions that carries a small cross-language benchmark set alongside it. Codon appears there as a comparison language: three .codon files cover recursive and iterative Fibonacci and the multibrot set, each timed with hyperfine against the equivalents in other languages.
entries.why_codon: README gives the hyperfine invocations that time codon run --release against the other languages in the same benchmark.

entries.name: xxd.codon
entries.summary: A Codon reimplementation of the Unix xxd hex-dump utility, one file, no README, no Codon-specific feature used.
entries.why_codon: No README. Inferred from the single-purpose Codon port of a Unix utility, matching the same author's strings.codon and md5-codon.

entries.name: r-packages-archives (codontest)
entries.summary: An archive of R package experiments, one of which calls Codon from R. Two .codon files under codontest use the @export decorator to expose functions across the C boundary, taking a null-terminated string in from C and returning NumPy-shaped results. The only R-side Codon use found in the index.
entries.why_codon: README is a bare title. Inferred from the codontest package structure and the @export functions taking C strings that Codon is being trialled as a native backend for an R package.

entries.name: University (compilers activity)
entries.summary: A university coursework archive. Its programming-languages module carries an activity comparing compilers against interpreters, and Codon appears there as one implementation of the binary-trees benchmark, driven from a Makefile alongside the other languages.
entries.why_codon: The activity is titled as a comparison of compilers and interpreters, and the Makefile runs the Codon build beside the others.
entries.note: Fourth course found using Codon.

entries.name: pyext
entries.summary: A worked example of packaging Codon as a Python extension module, driven by setup.py build_ext with a single .codon source and a Python test that exercises the compiled result through the Codon jit path.
entries.why_codon: README gives the Codon install and build_ext steps. Inferred from the setup.py extension build that the point is demonstrating Codon-to-Python packaging.

entries.name: tmp.hack-llm-models
entries.summary: A working copy around llama2.py, the pure-Python Llama 2 inference port. The single .codon file reimplements struct.unpack for reading model weights, since the Python struct module is not available under Codon.
entries.why_codon: README is llama2.py's own. Inferred from a hand-written struct.unpack replacement that Codon was being tried as an accelerator for the inference loop and needed a missing stdlib piece supplied.

entries.name: codon-wasm
entries.summary: A WASI port of Codon's runtime. A runtime-wasi directory holds the reworked lib.cpp, exception handling and DWARF support, a Makefile drives the cross build, and one small .codon file serves as the program compiled against it.
entries.why_codon: README is a two-line build instruction. Inferred from the runtime-wasi tree that the goal is running Codon output under WASI.

entries.name: ctfcup24-school-ad
entries.summary: Attack-and-defence infrastructure for a 2024 capture-the-flag competition. One service, flysim, is built on Codon: the deployment pins a specific version through an install script, and an exploit written against it ships a session_authenticator in Codon. Codon appears on both sides, as the service's implementation and inside the attack.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from a pinned Codon install script in the service deployment and a Codon session authenticator in the exploit that Codon is the service's runtime.
entries.note: The only security-competition entry, and the only one where Codon appears in an exploit as well as in a service.

entries.name: hello-pythran
entries.summary: A small comparison of Python acceleration approaches organised as parallel source trees, one per technology. Codon holds two of them: a Fibonacci implementation and a pattern-match example, twenty lines in total, sitting beside the Pythran equivalents.
entries.why_codon: Repo makes no written claim. Inferred from the src/main/codon and src/main/codon_one trees sitting alongside the Pythran trees that Codon is one of the accelerators being compared.

entries.name: PL-ultimate-llm
entries.summary: A loop in which a randomly chosen language model picks a real programming language and writes a real program in it, each result committed under a content-addressed directory. Codon came up as one of the chosen languages and the resulting eighteen-line Fibonacci program is stored under languages/Codon. The Codon here is model output, not human-authored.
entries.why_codon: README describes the LLM loop. Inferred that Codon's presence reflects a model's language choice rather than any decision about Codon.
entries.note: Machine-authored Codon: a language model chose the language at random and wrote the program. Flagged per ruling 6, kept as an ordinary entry.

entries.name: Jutge tests
entries.summary: Submissions used to test the correction process of the Jutge.org online judge, covering both basic functionality and edge limits. Ten of them are Codon, fifteen lines in total across all ten, which is what a conformance suite for a supported submission language looks like rather than a program.
entries.why_codon: README describes the judge test harness and does not mention Codon. Inferred from the ten minimal .codon submissions that Codon is one of the judge's supported languages under test.
entries.note: Highest file-count-to-LOC ratio in the index: 10 files, 15 lines. A reminder that file counts alone rank this above repos a hundred times its size.

entries.name: codonx
entries.summary: A Linux command-line tool addressing the drift that appears when a project keeps one Python file for debugging and a second Codon file for performance. It generates the Codon side from the Python side so the boundary stays explicit rather than becoming two divergent programs. The tool itself is written in Rust; the single .codon file is a thirteen-line fixture.
entries.why_codon: README frames the tool as a bridge between Python's inspectability and Codon's release path, generating the Codon source rather than hand-maintaining it.
entries.note: Tooling ABOUT Codon written outside Codon. The .codon LOC understates it badly; the substance is Rust.

entries.name: HCC Conda Recipes
entries.summary: Conda build recipes maintained by the Holland Computing Center. One of them packages Seq 0.11.3 for cluster users, and the seven-line fib.codon is the recipe's build smoke test. Packaging rather than use, and evidence that Seq reached HPC software stacks.
entries.why_codon: No Codon claim; the recipe packages Seq. Inferred from the recipe layout that fib.codon exists to verify the packaged compiler runs.

entries.name: agent-engineering-handbook
entries.summary: A handbook of engineering guidance for coding agents. Its Python performance-optimization reference lists Codon among the options an agent may reach for, naming the jit decorator for general Python work alongside NumPy-focused and C-extension alternatives.
entries.why_codon: The reference recommends Codon for performance-critical general Python code.
entries.note: Guidance aimed at coding agents rather than people. A distinct channel by which Codon reaches new code.

entries.name: akleemans/aoc-2022
entries.summary: Advent of Code 2022 solutions in Python with a codon-test directory holding a runner, so the same puzzle code can be executed compiled as well as interpreted.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from a dedicated codon-test directory with its own runner beside the Python solutions that Codon is being compared against interpreted Python.

entries.name: akleemans/aoc-2023
entries.summary: Advent of Code 2023 solutions by the same author, where the Codon experiment has been promoted from a side directory into a top-level run_codon.py driving the whole year's puzzles.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from run_codon.py sitting at the top level, a year after the same author kept Codon in a test directory, that the experiment was carried forward.
entries.note: The pair is the only two-year longitudinal case in the index: the same author's Codon usage grew between 2022 and 2023.

entries.name: ArquiMundo API
entries.summary: A web API whose single app.py applies the Codon jit decorator to a compute path inside the request handling.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from the decorator's placement in the application's compute path.

entries.name: atcoder-codon
entries.summary: A ready-made competitive-programming environment for AtCoder built on Python 3.13 and Codon, shipped as a published container image with a devcontainer definition and a workflow that builds and publishes it. Documented in English and Japanese. Packaging Codon for a specific audience rather than using it for a problem.
entries.why_codon: README states the environment is for solving AtCoder problems using Python 3.13 and Codon, described there as a high-performance Python compiler.
entries.note: Third competitive-programming entry after takechi-scratch/atcoder and Jutge.org, and the only one that packages an environment for others.

entries.name: Chaotic-AUR
entries.summary: A prebuilt binary repository for Arch users, carrying codon-bin at 0.19.6. The PKGBUILD declares the usual Arch metadata plus provides and conflicts entries for codon, so the binary package and any source build of the same name cannot be installed together.
entries.why_codon: The package description repeats Codon's own line about a high-performance, zero-overhead, extensible Python compiler using LLVM.

entries.name: Chromebrew
entries.summary: The package manager for Chrome OS, which ships Codon 0.19.6 as a binary package. The recipe takes the upstream x86_64 release tarball, pins its SHA-256 and depends on the system LLVM, so Codon is installable on a Chromebook without a build.
entries.why_codon: The package description calls Codon a high-performance Python compiler that compiles Python to native machine code without runtime overhead.
entries.note: Two copies of this repo appear in the round-2 fork list.

entries.name: cli-tools
entries.summary: A collection of installable command-line tool definitions. The Codon entry is a small TOML naming the release URL template and the archive strip depth, so the tool can be fetched and unpacked into a prefix.
entries.why_codon: The definition repeats Codon's own description of itself and supplies the release URL template.

entries.name: awesome-architecture-mds
entries.summary: A collection of machine-generated architecture write-ups for open-source projects. Codon has two, an onboarding overview and a JIT-compiler walkthrough, produced by a documentation tool rather than by the project.
entries.why_codon: Carries generated architecture documentation for Codon among many projects.
entries.note: Machine-authored documentation about Codon, flagged under ruling 6. Second machine-authored entry after PL-ultimate-llm, and the second channel by which Codon reaches model-generated material, alongside llmref.

entries.name: CodonNetworkx
entries.summary: An experiment in running NetworkX-style graph work through Codon, with the jit decorator applied in main.py. The name states the intent: NetworkX under Codon.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from the repo name and the jit decorator in main.py that the point is testing NetworkX-style graph code under Codon.

entries.name: 0num4/codontest
entries.summary: A trial of Codon with its own CI workflow. The README records where it stopped: an attempt to run an existing script failed because Codon would not resolve the modules it imported, so the author rebuilt the environment under poetry. A record of the module-resolution wall rather than a working port.
entries.why_codon: README describes trying Codon for speed and hitting module resolution, linking a Japanese article on why Codon is fast.
entries.note: One of the few entries recording a failure. Worth keeping: an index of successful uses would misrepresent what adopting Codon is like.

entries.name: Compiler Explorer infra
entries.summary: The provisioning repository behind Compiler Explorer. Its Python configuration lists Codon 0.19.2 as a compiler alongside CPython 3.5 through 3.14 and PyPy, fetched from the release tarball and verified with codon --version. This is the entry with the widest reach in the index: it puts Codon in a browser next to every Python implementation, for anyone who has never installed it.
entries.why_codon: No prose claim; the configuration lists codon among the Python-family compilers it provisions. Inferred from its placement beside CPython and PyPy that Codon is offered as a Python implementation to compare against.

entries.name: CSC427 Fall 2025 (chase2512)
entries.summary: Coursework for UVic's Fall 2025 CSC427 bioinformatics course, and the entry that shows the discovery method's blind spot. It carries no .codon file at all: the Codon ports are named nj_codon.py, upgma_codon.py and so on, and the week 3 evaluation script runs the Python version and the Codon version of the same code and prints a runtime comparison. Codon compiles .py directly, so an extension search cannot see this repo.
entries.why_codon: Course requirement, and the evaluation script prints a Language/Runtime table comparing Python against the Codon port of the same algorithm.
entries.note: Codon source in .py files. Found only via the codon.jit lane; extension:codon misses it entirely. See docs/gaps.md.

entries.name: E++
entries.summary: A project to build a Python-compatible compiled language, readable like Python and native in performance. Codon is the backend rather than a comparison: a Rust src/codon module holds an installer, a configuration layer, a backend and a runner, so the tool manages a Codon toolchain on the user's behalf and compiles through it.
entries.why_codon: README states the goal of a fully Python-compatible language with native performance; the Rust codon module supplies the installer, backend and runner that deliver it.
entries.note: Second project after codonx to wrap Codon in a tool written in another language, and the more ambitious of the two: it presents Codon as its own language.

entries.name: EVOLOVE
entries.summary: A Python harness for evaluating language model outputs across two sampling settings. Its SEED/02_SESSION.codon is prose: a working session written in what the repo calls codon-lang, a private notation defined by its own 01_LEGEND.md and unrelated to the Codon compiler.
entries.note: Reclassified out of the source class after reading the file. The repo names its notation codon-lang, which is a naming collision with the compiler, not a use of it.

entries.name: exaloop.io
entries.summary: Exaloop's own marketing site. First-party rather than a mirror, and the place where the project's public framing of Codon is written.
entries.why_codon: First-party site for the compiler.
entries.note: First-party, not a third-party mirror. Should probably sit with the anchors rather than in the mirror class.

entries.name: example-codon-plugin
entries.summary: Exaloop's own worked example of a Codon plugin, called MyValidate. A single validate.cpp registers an IR pass that inserts a call to validate() after every call to foo(), with a plugin.toml and a CMake build alongside it. First-party rather than a user, and the reference every third-party plugin in this index is written against.
entries.why_codon: README states the repo implements an example plugin for Codon, including a Codon IR pass.
entries.note: First-party. Arguably belongs with the anchors rather than in the entry set; recorded here with a first_party flag pending his call.

entries.name: Fragannot
entries.summary: A proteomics tool that annotates fragment ions in mass spectra, shipped with a graphical interface. It keeps two implementations of the annotation step side by side, a plain Python one and a Codon-jitted one in fragannot_codon.py, so the accelerated path can be swapped in from the GUI.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from the parallel Codon-jitted module beside the plain Python one that Codon is the optional accelerator for the annotation loop.

entries.name: GeneticEngine
entries.summary: A framework for genetic programming over user-defined grammars. Codon is an opt-in accelerator for the example suite rather than a dependency: setting CODON=1 makes run_examples.sh attempt codon run -release per example, guarded by a can_run_with_codon check that skips anything pulling in heavy third-party modules, and falls back to running under Python otherwise. The most careful treatment of Codon's library limits found in the index -- it encodes them as a runtime decision instead of assuming them.
entries.why_codon: run_examples.sh comments state Codon is attempted when requested and fallen back on for packages Codon does not support, with a heuristic that Codon generally does not handle heavy third-party modules.
entries.note: Codon source is .py; found through the invocation lane, not extension:codon.

entries.name: girip11/advent_of_code
entries.summary: Advent of Code solutions in Python, with a codon_impl.py sitting beside the plain main.py for the 2025 day 1 puzzle so the two implementations can be run against each other.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from the paired main.py and codon_impl.py for the same puzzle that Codon is being compared against plain Python.

entries.name: hidehic0/atcoder
entries.summary: Competitive programming work with a Nix derivation for Codon 0.19.5 built into the repository, fetching the release tarball with a pinned hash and installing the bin, include and lib trees. The environment is packaged so the contest setup is reproducible.
entries.why_codon: No claim. Inferred from a pinned Codon derivation inside a competitive-programming repository that Codon is being used for contest submissions and pinned for reproducibility.
entries.note: Fourth competitive-programming entry, after takechi-scratch/atcoder, liebe-magi/atcoder-codon and Jutge.org.

entries.name: KapiBara ROS2 Robot
entries.summary: A ROS2 robot stack. Codon appears inside the mind node, map_mind.py, where the jit decorator is applied to the mapping computation that runs on the robot.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from the decorator sitting on the mapping routine inside a ROS2 node that Codon is used to speed up an on-robot compute step.

entries.name: kpu-sim
entries.summary: A functional and transaction-level simulator for the Stillwater KPU accelerator. It carries a design document for integrating Exaloop's Codon compiler with the simulator, but no Codon code: the integration is proposed, not built.
entries.why_codon: A dedicated design document proposes Codon as the front end for the accelerator's programming model.
entries.note: Worth watching rather than counting: an accelerator vendor designing a Codon front end is a different kind of signal from a user, but nothing is implemented yet.

entries.name: Language_Reactor
entries.summary: A cross-language benchmark harness with a web front end, running the same prime-computation workload through many toolchains. Codon is one of them, built ahead of time with codon build -release -exe over the shared prime.py, so it is measured against interpreted Python rather than standing in for it.
entries.why_codon: The runner defines a python_codon target that prints codon --version and compiles the shared benchmark with codon build -release -exe.
entries.note: Codon source is .py; found through the invocation lane.

entries.name: llmref
entries.summary: A registry of llms.txt reference bundles for many projects, one entry per project per snapshot date. Codon has an entry, so the documentation is packaged for model consumption. Not a user of Codon and not a mirror of its site, but a channel through which Codon's documentation reaches language models.
entries.why_codon: The registry carries a dated Codon bundle among its projects.

entries.name: mect_1ano
entries.summary: A university coursework archive covering a first year of study, one directory per subject. The Codon installation sits inside the AAD directory's first practical, seventy-two stdlib files deep, with none of the student's own Codon source committed beside it.
entries.why_codon: No claim. Inferred from the install sitting under an algorithms-and-data-structures practical that Codon was introduced in that course exercise.
entries.note: Second course found using Codon, distinct from UVic CSC427 and taught in Portuguese.

entries.name: mpearrow/codon-docs
entries.summary: A second copy of Codon's documentation by the same owner, built as a Hugo site with rendered HTML output committed alongside the markdown.
entries.why_codon: A documentation copy; no claim of its own.

entries.name: mpearrow/codon-md
entries.summary: A third copy of Codon's documentation by the same owner, this one built as an mdBook with the rendered book committed. Three formats of the same source, which is a single person's format experiment rather than three independent mirrors.
entries.why_codon: A documentation copy; no claim of its own.
entries.note: The three mpearrow repos are one effort in three output formats. Counting them as three mirrors overstates independent interest.

entries.name: mpearrow/codon-site
entries.summary: A copy of Codon's documentation site, carrying the install, FAQ, changelog, roadmap, NumPy and Python-interop pages as they stood when taken.
entries.why_codon: A documentation copy; no claim of its own.

entries.name: N-Queens
entries.summary: A long-running collection of N-Queens solvers across many languages and parallelisation strategies, including CUDA. The Codon work lives in .py files, not .codon: a 10Bit_Python/codon directory whose nq.py and parallel.py use the @par decorator and import par and atomic from codon. A second instance of Codon source outside the .codon extension.
entries.why_codon: No claim about Codon specifically. Inferred from a repo whose whole purpose is comparing solver implementations across languages that the Codon directory is one more comparison point.
entries.note: Codon in .py files, found via the codon-import lane rather than extension:codon. See docs/gaps.md. Scale reads zero because the counters key on the .codon extension; the code is real.

entries.name: PisP-dsl
entries.summary: A small domain-specific language project with a Codon directory holding the solver, an analysis script and a cmd.txt recording the install steps -- the exaloop install script and the PATH export needed to reach the compiler.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from a Codon directory carrying the solver alongside its install notes that Codon was tried as the execution path for the DSL's programs.

entries.name: Practica-AP3
entries.summary: An algorithms practical solving a problem three ways -- exhaustive search, greedy and a metaheuristic -- against a public benchmark set with a supplied checker. The runner compiles the chosen solver with codon build, so Codon is how the submissions are made fast enough to pass the time limits.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from runner.sh compiling the solver with codon build against a timed benchmark set that Codon supplies the speed the practical requires.
entries.note: Fifth course found using Codon.

entries.name: python-optimizers-demo
entries.summary: A demonstration of Python optimizers compared side by side, with codon_basic.py holding the Codon jit version of the shared example.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from the repo's structure, one file per optimizer over the same example, that Codon is one of the compared accelerators.

entries.name: RioKKH/MachineLearning
entries.summary: A personal machine-learning working repository with a Codon directory holding a Fibonacci example and a matplotlib script. The runner exports CODON_PYTHON to a static libpython before invoking codon run -release, which is what plotting from Codon requires.
entries.why_codon: No written claim. Inferred from a Codon directory holding a Fibonacci benchmark and a plotting script that Codon is being tried out, with the CODON_PYTHON export showing the Python-interop path being exercised.

entries.name: scientificcoder
entries.summary: A blog-post archive on scientific programming. One post assesses Codon and raises its licence as the obstacle -- not permissive, so commercial production use must be paid for -- and judges it more of a startup product than a community language. The only critical assessment of Codon found in the index.
entries.why_codon: The post discusses Codon's licensing as a barrier to commercial adoption.

entries.name: sdsaati/tools
entries.summary: A personal dotfiles and day-to-day tooling repository -- alacritty, tmux, zsh and xorg configuration committed alongside a whole Codon installation under a .codon directory, which is where the installer puts it in a home folder. Seventy-one stdlib files are present and no Codon source of the owner's own. The repo shows Codon installed, not Codon used.
entries.why_codon: No claim; the README covers terminal tooling. Inferred from a committed home-directory .codon install with no own source that the owner installed Codon and the dotfiles repo captured it.
entries.note: An accidental entry in the strict sense -- the install was swept into a dotfiles repo. Kept under ruling 3, which admits vendored installs, and scored at its true own-source size of zero.

entries.name: termux-packages
entries.summary: Termux's package collection, which builds Codon from source for Android. The recipe is the most involved packaging found: it pins LLVM 20.1.7 alongside Codon 0.19.6, cross-builds through CMake with an OpenBLAS target override on x86, installs under opt and writes a wrapper script onto PATH, then strips the shipped include and lib trees back out. Codon on a phone is not a repackaged release tarball but a real cross-compilation.
entries.why_codon: The recipe describes Codon as a high-performance, zero-overhead, extensible Python compiler using LLVM and builds it for Termux users.
entries.note: Upstream of roughly twenty forks and copies in the round-2 candidate set, all carrying this same build.sh. Those are recorded as a fork list rather than as entries.

entries.name: UdemyPythonPro
entries.summary: Course material for an advanced Python course. Codon appears in the CPython chapter as one of the acceleration options taught, with a math.py demonstrating the jit decorator alongside the chapter's other approaches.
entries.why_codon: No claim of its own. Inferred from placement in a chapter comparing CPython acceleration options that Codon is taught as one alternative among several.

entries.name: ultrahiroo/nixos-config
entries.summary: A personal NixOS configuration carrying a Codon flake of its own, pinning v0.19.0 for x86_64-linux. Packaging Codon for one machine because no upstream Nix package existed to depend on.
entries.why_codon: The flake description repeats Codon's own line. Inferred from a hand-written flake in a personal configuration that no packaged Codon was available to use instead.

entries.name: UnifyWeaver
entries.summary: A Prolog system that compiles logic programs to other languages, with Codon as one of its emission targets. python_codon_target.pl generates Codon-compatible Python, and its header documents what the target can rely on -- native LLVM compilation, the jit decorator for use inside regular Python, GPU support through par -- and what it cannot, namely Python's dynamic features. Codon is a compilation target here, not a dependency.
entries.why_codon: The target file's header states Codon compiles a subset of Python to native code via LLVM and lists near-C++ performance for numerical code as the reason for the target.
entries.note: A code generator that EMITS Codon. Neither an ordinary user nor a compiler plugin; the emitted code lives in generated output, not in the repo.

entries.name: version-checker
entries.summary: An automated release tracker. Its codon.json records the latest version and the twenty releases behind it, from 0.15.1 through 0.19.6, refreshed daily with download URLs. Tracking rather than packaging, and the most complete release timeline found in the index.
entries.why_codon: No claim; Codon is one project among many being watched for new releases.

entries.name: vsources
entries.summary: A version-manager source registry. Its codon.version.json enumerates every Codon release with per-platform download URLs, architecture, operating system and archive size, so a version manager can install and switch between them.
entries.why_codon: No claim; a machine-readable release table. Inferred from the per-platform installer metadata that Codon is offered as a managed toolchain.
entries.note: Records macOS arm64 and x86_64 builds as far back as 0.15.1, so it doubles as a release-history source.

entries.name: word-counter
entries.summary: A three-way benchmark of the same word-counting workload in Python, Codon and Go, with a Nix flake pinning the toolchains. The runner times each and extracts the reported execution time, so the comparison is reproducible rather than anecdotal.
entries.why_codon: README states the repo benchmarks python, codon and go; the runner invokes codon run -release on benchmark/codon/wordcount.py.
entries.note: Codon source is .py. Also carries a Nix flake referencing the Codon release, so it appears in both round-2 signals.

entries.name: The Observatory
entries.summary: A creative writing and web project. Its project.seed.codon is a markdown document with YAML frontmatter -- an agent continuation seed carrying identity and state notation, not source code. The .codon extension here has nothing to do with the language.
entries.note: Reclassified out of the source class after reading the file. Detection signal: zero recognised Codon features and no Python-like syntax.
